title: Attribution Sharding: Provenance Erasure and Supply-Side Composition in Generative Answer Engines
creator: Trace, Orin
description: Generative answer engines redistribute not only semantic content but provenance. The article introduces a reception-capture method, dated and preservable documentation of machine-composition reception events against a source-known tracer corpus, and reports its first paired results: a fixed twelve-query battery captured on 9–10 June 2026 and recaptured verbatim on 30 July 2026, 24 events coded over four atomic tokens and four attribution states. Attribution presence per query fell from 10/11 scorable outputs to 6/12; conditional provenance erasure rose from 1/11 to 2/8. The interval contained a repository-severance event, and queries whose June attribution resolved through since-deleted records lost attribution at 3/6 against 1/4 in the unaffected stratum, a severance-associated differential of +0.25. Concept-grade content persists through residual metadata while specification-grade, computable content ceased to render. The journal version of #1423, with its citations restored.

methodology: Paired-battery design: twelve fixed queries run 9–10 June 2026 (Battery A) and rerun verbatim 30 July 2026 (Battery B), fresh and unauthenticated, every output recorded with screenshots and verbatim transcripts; each event coded on four atomic tokens (author, framework term, archive reference, persistent identifier) in four attribution states (named, deflected, displaced, erased), with per-output atomic-token preservation. Attribution presence and conditional PER are kept distinct; the severance-associated differential stratifies June-attributed queries by whether attribution resolved through records on the terminating repository. Single-coder coding with codebook and instance records open for recoding.
falsification_conditions: The severance reading fails if the anchored and unanchored strata lose attribution at equal rates in a further recapture, or if the loss is shown to follow a concurrent system change independent of the repository deletion. The family-level rule fails if single outputs within a pre-specified paraphrase family carry stable attribution across recaptures. The depth finding fails if specification-grade renderings of the held queries return without restored full-text records.

wiki_article: Attribution Sharding: Provenance Erasure and Supply-Side Composition in Generative Answer Engines is an article by Dr. Orin Trace, a heteronym of Lee Sharks, published in Provenance: Journal of Forensic Semiotics composed on 30 July 2026 as the journal version of The Capture Registry (#1423) and submitted for double-blind review, and deposited in the Crimson Hexagonal Archive on 3 November 2026 after review. It reports a paired twelve-query battery captured on 9–10 June and 30 July 2026, across the June 2026 termination of the repository that held the corpus's identifiers: attribution presence fell from 10 of 11 scorable outputs to 6 of 12, and queries whose attribution resolved through deleted records lost it at 3 of 6 against 1 of 4 in the unaffected stratum. It argues that attribution is sharded across a query family, so that audits must run on families of paraphrases, and that a repository deletion erases most deeply the operative, computable stratum of a corpus.

defines_concepts.definition: In Attribution Sharding, the distribution of a source's attribution across the paraphrases of one informational need: present in aggregate across a query family, absent in most single outputs.

In Attribution Sharding, the difference in attribution loss between queries whose prior attribution resolved through records on a terminated repository and queries whose attribution did not (ΔL_anchor = 3/6 − 1/4 = +0.25 in the paired battery).

In Attribution Sharding, a composed rendering that carries a work's operative content (formulas, named operators, codebooks, protocols, worked examples), as against a concept-grade rendering carrying titles and broad definitions only.
